content.content:
# Bun Rust Rewrite: Summary

## Why Rewrite in Rust?

Bun faced persistent stability issues stemming from mixing garbage-collected JavaScript values with manually-managed memory in Zig. The blog lists 12 specific bugs from v1.3.14 alone—use-after-free crashes, double-frees, and memory leaks. While Zig enabled Bun's initial rapid development, its lack of built-in memory safety guarantees made preventing these issues difficult. Rust's borrow checker and RAII (automatic cleanup via `Drop`) provide compiler-enforced guarantees against these entire classes of bugs.

## Current Status

The Rust rewrite has been **completed and merged into the main branch**. All 1,448 Zig files were translated to Rust across 6,502 commits over 11 days (May 4-14, 2026). The full test suite passes on all six supported platforms (Linux x64/arm64, macOS x64/arm64, Windows x64/arm64), with approximately 1.4 million test assertions verified.

## Release Timeline

**Bun v1.4.0 will be the first Rust-based release.** The post states: "Bun v1.3.14 was the last version of Bun written in Zig." The Rust version is currently available as a canary build (`bun upgrade --canary`), with general availability expected imminently, though no specific date is provided.

| `vitest`                       | Removed in the common node-mode case because `vite-plus` provides it transitively. Kept or added only when [directly required](#when-vitest-is-directly-required).      |

### Version Selection

- `vite-plus` is pinned to the concrete version of the CLI running the
  migration, never the `latest` dist-tag.
- The `vite` alias targets `@voidzero-dev/vite-plus-core` from the same Vite+
  release.
- A catalog-backed manifest may contain `catalog:` or a named catalog
  reference. Migration keeps the reference and updates the referenced catalog
  value to the concrete toolchain target.
- Deliberate protocol pins are preserved: `workspace:`, `file:`, `link:`,
  `npm:`, `github:`, Git URLs, and HTTP URLs.
- Migration reconciles every workspace package, not only the root manifest.
  Shared overrides and catalogs stay at the workspace root; dependencies that
  provide a peer belong in each package that needs them.

### Vite and Overrides

Package-manager overrides do not create dependency edges by themselves. Under
pnpm, a package that lists `vite-plus` in `dependencies` or `devDependencies`
but has no `vite` entry anywhere (`dependencies`, `devDependencies`,
`optionalDependencies`, or `peerDependencies`) lets pnpm auto-install upstream
Vite to satisfy Vitest's required `vite` peer, splitting the project across
separate Vite+, Vite, and Vitest instances. To prevent this, `vp migrate` adds
the missing `vite` entry to `devDependencies` of every such package; the
workspace override then redirects it to Vite+ core.

Related rules:

- A direct `vite` declaration is never removed merely because a root override
  exists.
- Plain or stale aliases are normalized; named catalog references are kept.
- The direct-entry rule above is pnpm-specific. Bun mirrors its core alias as
  a direct dependency for its peer resolver, and npm browser-provider layouts
  may need a top-level `vite` edge so nested Vitest packages can resolve
  `vite`.

content.text:
Probably yes, eventually — but not soon, and not by your choice; it'll be when the toolchain itself makes it unnecessary. The docs don't state a timeline (I checked), so here's my read of the mechanics:

The override exists because the whole JS ecosystem — vitest, the TanStack plugins, every Vite plugin — declares `vite` as its peer dependency, while Vite+ ships its core under a different name (`@voidzero-dev/vite-plus-core`). The alias is the bridge that makes all those packages resolve to Vite+ instead of upstream Vite. That bridge stays necessary as long as those two facts hold.

It goes away in one of two futures: either VoidZero folds the Vite+ core back into the `vite` package itself in some future major release (Vite+ is built on Vite, so upstreaming is the natural endgame — at that point the alias is a no-op and `vp migrate` would presumably remove it), or the ecosystem starts accepting `vite-plus-core` as a peer directly, which is much less likely to happen uniformly. Given Vite+ is still at 0.2.x, I'd expect the override to be a fixture through the 0.x era and to disappear as part of a scripted migration when the packaging story stabilizes — not something you'll delete by hand. The practical takeaway: treat it as toolchain-managed plumbing, keep it in lockstep with the `vite-plus` version (like we just did), and let `vp migrate` handle its retirement.

Ah, the `"typescript": "$typescript"` one — yes, and honestly that one looks removable already, not just eventually.

Looking at the actual dependency tree, only one thing pulls in TypeScript besides your direct dependency: `@voidzero-dev/vite-plus-core`, and it declares it as an optional peer dependency with the range `^5.0.0 || ^6.0.0 || ^7.0.0`. With the current tree, that risk isn't materializing — nothing here declares a range that excludes 7. Where it still earns its keep is as future-proofing: if you later add a dependency that hard-pins TS 5, the override silently prevents a second TypeScript from appearing. That's a one-line cost for a real (if unlikely) protection, so I'd personally leave it, but removing it today would change nothing in the resolved tree. Strictly, no — today it's a no-op, and it's arguably a small liability.

Here's the situation: everything in the tree already agrees on exactly 4.1.10 without any forcing. `vite-plus` depends on `vitest` at exact version 4.1.10, `@vitest/coverage-v8@4.1.10` peer-requires exactly `vitest: 4.1.10`, and your direct devDependency is the exact pin `"vitest": "4.1.10"`. With every declaration exact and identical, npm resolves a single deduped copy whether the override exists or not.

Your direct pin is the right mechanism and needs to stay — the Vite+ docs say a direct `vitest` at the bundled version is kept precisely when a dependency has a non-optional vitest peer, which `@vitest/coverage-v8` is. But the docs' pattern is the direct pin, not an override on top of it.

The override isn't just redundant — it's a third copy of the version number to keep in lockstep. The failure mode it invites: you upgrade `vite-plus` to a release that bundles vitest 4.1.11, update the devDependency, and if the override is forgotten at 4.1.10 it would force vite-plus's own vitest *down* beneath it. So it protects against nothing that the exact pins don't already handle, while adding a place to make a mistake.

I'd remove it and keep the direct `"vitest": "4.1.10"` devDependency. Same verification as last time would confirm the lockfile resolution is unchanged — want me to?

# Vite+ Migration Guide Summary

## Coverage
This guide addresses migrating existing projects from separate tooling (Vite, Vitest, Oxlint, Oxfmt, ESLint, Prettier) into the unified Vite+ platform.

## Key Commands
- `vp migrate` — consolidates split tooling setups
- `vp migrate <path>` — targets a specific directory
- `vp migrate --no-interactive` — runs without prompts
- Optional flags: `--agent`, `--editor`, `--hooks`

## Migration Steps
The process "updates project dependencies, rewrites imports where needed, merges tool-specific config into `vite.config.ts`, updates scripts to the Vite+ command surface" and formats the project. Afterward, run `vp install`, `vp check`, `vp test`, and `vp build`.

## Vitest Handling
Vite+ re-exports Vitest 4.x under `vite-plus/test*`. Import statements change from `vitest` to `vite-plus/test`. Browser-mode providers (Playwright, WebdriverIO) remain optional dependencies and must be installed separately if used.

## TypeScript & package.json
The guide doesn't discuss package.json overrides or TypeScript-specific considerations explicitly. However, it notes that "most projects will require further manual adjustments after running `vp migrate`."

## Post-Migration Maintenance
The recommended workflow emphasizes running validation checks after migration to confirm the setup works correctly.

# Commit Hooks

Use `vp config` to install commit hooks, and `vp staged` to run checks on staged files.

## Overview

Vite+ supports commit hooks and staged-file checks without additional tooling.

Use:

- `vp config` to set up project hooks and related integrations
- `vp staged` to run checks against the files currently staged in Git

If you use [`vp create`](/guide/create) or [`vp migrate`](/guide/migrate), Vite+ prompts you to set this up for your project automatically.

## Commands

### `vp config`

`vp config` configures Vite+ for the current project. It installs Git hooks, sets up the hook directory, and can also handle related project integration such as agent setup. By default, hooks are written to `.vite-hooks`:

```bash
vp config
vp config --hooks-dir .vite-hooks
vp config --no-hooks
vp config --no-agent
```

Use `--no-hooks` when you want `vp config` to leave existing Git hook setup unchanged. Use
`--no-agent` when you want it to skip updates to existing coding agent instruction files. You
can pass both flags when you want `vp config` to skip both setup steps.

You can also set `VITE_GIT_HOOKS=0` to disable hook installation from lifecycle scripts such as
`prepare` or `postinstall`.

### `vp staged`

`vp staged` runs staged-file checks using the `staged` config from `vite.config.ts`. If you set up Vite+ to handle your commit hooks, it will automatically run when you commit your local changes.

```bash
vp staged
vp staged --verbose
vp staged --fail-on-changes
```

## Configuration

Define staged-file checks in the `staged` block in `vite.config.ts`:

```ts [vite.config.ts]
import { defineConfig } from 'vite-plus';

export default defineConfig({
  staged: {
    '*.{js,ts,tsx,vue,svelte}': 'vp check --fix',
  },
});
```

This is the default Vite+ approach and should replace separate `lint-staged` configuration in most projects. Because `vp staged` reads from `vite.config.ts`, your staged-file checks stay in the same place as your lint, format, test, build, and task-runner config.

Mostly compliant, but the audit turned up three real deviations and one minor one:

**1. The `staged` config doesn't match the documented pattern — and it's the cause of the hook failure we hit.** The docs (commit-hooks.md, troubleshooting.md, and the migrate guide) all show a single command: `'*': 'vp check --fix'` or `'*.{js,ts,tsx,...}': 'vp check --fix'`. Your config runs two separate commands (`["vp fmt --write", "vp lint --fix"]`) on a TS-only glob. Besides being nonstandard, that's what blew up when the only staged TS file was the ignored `routeTree.gen.ts` — `vp fmt` with an explicitly empty target list errors out, whereas `vp check --fix` is designed to handle the "everything filtered out" case.

**2. No `lazyPlugins` wrapper.** Your `vite.config.ts` imports and instantiates all plugins (TanStack Start, Nitro, React, Tailwind, Babel) at the top level. The troubleshooting guide recommends wrapping them in `lazyPlugins(() => [...])` so that metadata-only commands — `vp lint`, `vp fmt`, `vp staged`, editor integration — don't evaluate heavy plugin factories on every invocation. With Nitro and TanStack Start in the list, that's meaningful overhead on every commit hook run.

**3. `engines.node: ">=18.0.0"` is stale.** The toolchain around it has moved on: Vite+ core's peers expect Node 20.19+/22.12+, and the docs note npm-based staged pass-through needs Node ≥ 22.14. Claiming Node 18 support is a promise the stack can't keep.

**4. (Minor) Redundant scripts.** `typecheck: tsc`, `lint`, `format`, and `format:check` all duplicate what `vp check` already does in one pass (Oxfmt + Oxlint + tsgolint type checks, since you have `typeCheck: true`). Harmless, but the docs position `vp check` as the single entry point, and even suggest migrating scripts to `vite.config.ts` tasks entirely.
